🍎 Lesson plan · 🌱 Basics · Lesson 3

Lesson plan: Neural Networks

The brain-inspired idea behind modern AI, explained simply.

By the end of the lesson, students can

  • describe a neural network as many simple artificial neurons arranged in layers;
  • explain what one neuron does with its inputs, weights, bias and activation function;
  • explain that learning means adjusting the weights, little by little, to make the error smaller.

Warm-up

Your brain has about 86 billion neurons. What do you think one neuron does on its own?

Collect guesses. Then explain that an artificial neuron is much simpler: it mostly multiplies and adds numbers. The power comes from connecting very many of them.

Reading

Students read the lesson “Neural Networks”. Students look for the four things one neuron does, and for the names of the three kinds of layers.

Activity: Mini-lab “Play with a neuron”

  1. Students open the mini-lab in lesson 3 and read the neuron's question: “Should I go to the park?”
  2. They read the sum under the sliders and check it with a calculator: multiply each input by its weight, then add the bias.
  3. They fill in the worksheet's table: change one slider at a time and write down the output and the decision.
  4. Pairs explain what a negative weight does to the decision.

For students who finish early

Fast finishers find settings where the neuron says “yes” with no sun at all, and explain which slider made the difference.

Discussion questions

  • Artificial neural networks were inspired by the brain. In what ways are they different from a real brain?
  • Why do the biggest networks need so much data and computing power to train?
  • Early layers find edges, later layers find whole objects. Why might building up step by step work better than looking for a cat in one go?
  • If nobody sets the weights by hand, who is responsible when a network makes a mistake?

Exit ticket

Name the three kinds of layers in a neural network, and say what each one does.

Quick check. During training, what does backpropagation do?
Right answer: Works out how to nudge each weight to make the error smaller

Easier and harder

Easier. Give the neuron's sum as a line with a gap: 0.90 × 1.5 + 0.20 × 2.5 − 1.5 = ___, and allow a calculator.

Harder. Students design a neuron of their own on paper, with three inputs for a decision of their own (for example, “Should I go to football practice?”), choose the weights and the bias, and explain each choice.
